newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Lyonnaise, Suez to form utility power.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lyonnaise, Suez to form utility power.

text.p: France's Lyonnaise des Eaux said on Friday that the diversified utility would take over holding company Cie de Suez to create a world heavyweight in utilities and services.
Lyonnaise chairman Jerome Monod told Europe 1 radio that the larger group would absorb Suez, a financial services and utilities company, through a friendly "merger-takeover".
The combined giant will focus on four core businesses -- energy, water distribution, waste management and communications.
Lyonnaise's "mission is to conquer the world", said Monod.

The companies, two of France's top corporate players, were due to announce at 1630 GMT on Friday details of the deal that ends the independence of Suez, set up in the 19th century to build the Suez Canal, a glory of French engineering.
Trading in the two companies' shares was suspended on the Paris bourse on Friday ahead of the announcement.
The combined group, to be called Suez Lyonnaise des Eaux, would give shareholders "a very big world actor that will be a leader in its activities and enjoy high visibility", Monod said.

He said the aim was to create a company that would boast annual turnover of 200 billion francs ($35 billion) and a stock market capitalisation of 75 billion francs. It would have the "resources to invest" around 17 billion francs from its first year of operation.

Under the deal, markets expect Suez shareholders to get 20 Lyonnaise shares for 41 Suez and a special dividend payout of around 3.8 billion francs or 24 francs per share. Monod has promised that the merged group will boost profits and cashflow.
The boards of the two companies were meeting on Friday to approve terms of the link-up, which has already won the nod from the Lyonnaise board.
Lyonnaise, which has activities in water distribution, construction and communications, has been pushing the deal as an operation that will give it extra muscle to expand abroad.

But by focusing on the four core activities, analysts say Lyonnaise's construction activities and most of the financial and industrial holdings controlled by Suez -- apart from Belgian energy and services giant Tractebel -- could be up for sale.

Lyonnaise is twice the size of Suez in terms of shareholders funds and one third bigger in share capitalisation. Suez, once one of France's grandest corporate institutions, fell victim in the early 1990s to a property slump.

Disgruntled Suez shareholders forced out the previous chairman Gerard Worms after the group posted a four billion franc 1995 loss and installed Gerard Mestrallet to turn round the overly diversified colossus.

Mestrallet swiftly sold crown jewels such as investment bank Banque Indosuez and fund manager Gartmore, and the ailing real estate portfolio was disposed of, leaving Suez with more than five billion francs in cash.
But he held on to a 63-percent stake in Belgian holding company, Societe Generale de Belgique, which groups some choice industrial and financial assets.

Ironically, it now appears SGB may have turned out to be the saviour of Suez, as financial analysts say the industrial logic to the merger could lie in Mestrallet's move to focus on utilities and abandon financial services.

SGB has a controlling stake in Tractebel, which specialises in electricity, gas, water and environmental services. It has operations in cable television, property, infrastructure and industrial installations -- areas which overlap with Lyonnaise.

Lyonnaise, under Monod, had set its sights on international expansion in utilities but lacked the financial strength to fund that growth. So a link-up would inject capital from Suez's cash hoard even after the dividend sweetener to Suez shareholders.
Lyonnaise shares closed on Thursday at 540 francs. Suez shares finished at 281.3 francs per share. ($ = 5.789 French Francs)
